set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 35
set1.q: Which type of retinal detachment is the most common?
opts: Congenital
Not one of the three types described.
Rhegmatogenous
Correct. Full-thickness retinal breaks let liquefied vitreous behind the retina.
Traction
That follows proliferative diabetic retinopathy and is less common.
Exudative
That accompanies systemic disease or a tumour.
Combined traction and exudative
Not the commonest presentation.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 40
set1.q: In a true blowout fracture, which wall gives way most often?
opts: The posterior wall
Not described as the site.
The superior orbital rim
The rim is the second mechanism, not the wall that fails.
The orbital floor
Correct. Raised orbital pressure blows out the floor most frequently, or the medial wall.
The lateral wall
Not the wall that gives way first.
The orbital roof
Not the wall that gives way first.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 47
set1.q: A patient with a basilar skull fracture has a cerebrospinal fluid leak. What follows?
opts: Repeat computed tomography in one week
That does not address the leak.
Neurosurgery consult and admission
Correct. The leak is what forces both.
Discharge with outpatient follow-up
A leak is not managed as an outpatient.
Ophthalmology consult and observation
The relevant specialty is neurosurgery.
Antibiotics alone, then discharge
Antibiotics here are themselves controversial.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 18
set1.q: Which instruction must a patient with a corneal abrasion never be given?
opts: Return if symptoms worsen
Re-examination is part of care.
Consider patching for comfort
Patching may help the pain.
Avoid rubbing the eye
Reasonable advice after an abrasion.
Take home topical anaesthetic drops for pain
Correct. They delay healing, mask worsening symptoms and can cause a corneal ulcer.
Use the topical antibiotic as prescribed
That is the treatment.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 47
set1.q: What is the limitation of computed tomography of the orbits in basilar skull fracture?
opts: It cannot show a cerebrospinal fluid leak at all
Not the stated limitation.
It is contraindicated after head trauma
It is the imaging of choice.
It requires contrast that may be nephrotoxic
Contrast is not the issue here.
It cannot be done in an unconscious patient
It can.
The fracture is not always evident on it
Correct. A normal scan does not exclude it.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43
set1.q: Why is ophthalmology consulted for a true blowout fracture even without entrapment?
opts: Because every fracture needs operative repair
Many do not.
Because the optic nerve is always damaged
It is not always involved.
To arrange spectacles for the diplopia
Not the reason for consultation.
To exclude a basilar skull fracture
That is a separate assessment.
About 30% sustain a significant globe injury
Correct. The globe has to be assessed.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set1.q: Over what period does most rebleeding after hyphema occur?
opts: Rebleeding is not a recognised complication
It is the complication management aims to prevent.
The first 72 hours
Correct. That is when a secondary haemorrhage is most likely.
The first 24 hours only
The window is longer than a day.
Between one and two weeks
Later than the peak risk.
After the first month
Well outside the peak risk.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 44
set1.q: Why is a basilar skull fracture often identified from indirect signs?
opts: It often produces no symptoms of its own
Correct. The indirect signs are what give it away.
The fracture is always visible on plain films
It is not, and radiographs are not the test.
It never causes bleeding
Bleeding into soft tissue is one of the signs.
Patients are always unconscious
That is not what makes it silent.
The signs appear within minutes
Timing is not the reason.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 26
set1.q: What proportion of full-thickness lid lacerations come with a corneal laceration or globe rupture?
opts: About one in ten
Far lower than the true association.
About one quarter
Lower than the true association.
Almost none
The association is strong.
About two thirds
Correct. Always look underneath a full-thickness lid cut.
About one in twenty
Far lower than the true association.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 33
set1.q: A patient has a periorbital haematoma with no history of injury. Which cause should be sought?
opts: Contact lens overwear
It does not cause orbital bleeding.
A previous hyphema
Not a listed cause of spontaneous orbital bleeding.
Anticoagulants, eye surgery or orbital varices
Correct. It is not always traumatic.
A corneal abrasion earlier in the week
That does not bleed into the orbit.
Seasonal allergy
It does not cause orbital bleeding.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 27
set1.q: Why may a facial laceration be left open for 24 hours before closure?
opts: The face is highly vascular
Correct. That vascularity is what permits the delay.
It reduces the need for antibiotics
Not the stated reason.
It allows swelling to resolve first
Not the reason given for the face.
It improves the cosmetic result in every case
Not the stated reason.
It is required by tetanus prophylaxis
Unrelated to wound timing.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 8
set1.q: Which history point matters because surgery may follow?
opts: The patient's usual spectacle prescription
Not what determines operative timing.
Whether the patient wears contact lenses at night
Relevant to infection, not to operative timing.
Family history of glaucoma
Not relevant to acute trauma management.
When the patient last ate and drank
Correct. Nil-by-mouth status shapes the anaesthetic plan.
Which eye is dominant
It does not change acute management.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 31
set1.q: A patient has an orbital contusion after a blow to the face. What must be excluded?
opts: Allergic conjunctivitis
Unrelated to the injury.
Retinoblastoma
Not a traumatic consideration.
Brain trauma
Correct. The force that bruised the orbit reaches the brain.
Thyroid eye disease
Not an acute traumatic consideration.
Chronic open-angle glaucoma
Not what trauma raises acutely.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 35
set1.q: Which event usually precedes a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
opts: Posterior vitreous detachment
Correct. The vitreous separates first, then traction opens a retinal break.
Central retinal artery occlusion
A different disease entirely.
Acute angle closure
Unrelated to the retinal break.
Optic neuritis
Unrelated to the retinal break.
Corneal ulceration
A surface disease, unrelated.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set1.q: When is intraocular pressure NOT measured in a patient with hyphema?
opts: When the hyphema fills less than half the chamber
Size does not change whether pressure is measured.
When the patient is under sixteen
Age is not the exclusion.
When the injury was more than a day ago
Timing is not the exclusion.
Pressure is measured in every case
There is one clear exception.
When a penetrating globe injury is suspected
Correct. Pressing on an open globe risks extruding its contents.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 36
set1.q: Within what period must a patient with a retinal detachment see ophthalmology?
opts: Within 2 to 3 days
Later than required.
At the next routine clinic
Far later than required.
Only if the vision worsens
Referral does not wait on deterioration.
Within 24 hours
Correct. The referral is immediate.
Within one week
Later than required.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 3
set1.q: A 24-year-old man arrives after a workshop explosion with an obviously injured right eye and noisy breathing. What comes first?
opts: Visual acuity in both eyes
Acuity matters, but not before the airway.
A shield over the injured eye
The shield comes once the patient is stable.
Computed tomography of the orbits
Imaging follows resuscitation.
Ophthalmology consultation
The consult is called after the primary survey.
Airway, breathing and circulation
Correct. The eye waits until the patient is stable.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17
set1.q: Which history makes globe rupture more likely at lower force?
opts: Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis
It does not affect eye wall strength.
Previous corneal abrasion
A healed abrasion does not weaken the wall.
Previous intraocular surgery
Correct. Old incisions leave a permanent weak point.
A history of migraine
It does not weaken the eye wall.
Long-standing myopia alone
Myopia predisposes to detachment rather than rupture.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set1.q: Why is oral aminocaproic acid used in hyphema?
opts: It dilates the pupil to rest the ciliary body
That is the cycloplegic's role.
It slows clot breakdown
Correct. It is an antifibrinolytic.
It lowers the intraocular pressure
Pressure is treated with other agents.
It reverses anticoagulation
It is not a reversal agent.
It prevents secondary infection
It has no antimicrobial action.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 8
set1.q: A patient with ocular trauma is intoxicated and cannot give a history. Where should the account come from?
opts: The examination findings alone
Findings do not establish mechanism or velocity.
The transferring service's diagnosis
That is not a substitute for the history.
Family, friends or bystanders
Correct. The circumstance of injury still has to be established.
The medical record alone
It will not carry the circumstance of this injury.
Waiting until the patient sobers
Delay costs time in an injury that may need surgery.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 22
set1.q: When does a corneal foreign body need ophthalmology rather than removal at the bedside?
opts: When the patient wears contact lenses
Lens wear alone does not change who removes it.
When there is a rust ring
A rust ring is removed with a burr.
When it has been present more than a day
Duration alone is not the trigger.
When the patient is a child
Age alone is not the trigger.
When it may have passed through the cornea
Correct. That is an open globe, not a surface foreign body.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 22
set1.q: A rust ring remains after a metallic foreign body is removed. How is it dealt with?
opts: A cotton-tipped applicator
That is for conjunctival foreign bodies.
Leaving it to resorb
It does not resorb on its own.
Topical chelating drops
Not the described method.
A burr tip drill
Correct. That is how a rust ring comes out.
Repeated irrigation with saline
Irrigation will not lift a rust ring.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 14
set1.q: A 30-year-old has a distorted pupil pulled toward a corneal wound, a flat anterior chamber and a soft eye. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Open globe injury
Correct. Those three findings together define a full-thickness defect.
Corneal abrasion
An abrasion leaves the chamber formed and the pupil round.
Traumatic iritis
Iritis does not flatten the anterior chamber.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage
That is confined to the surface.
Orbital contusion
Contusion is soft tissue swelling without a globe defect.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 24
set1.q: A patient struck in the eye has blood layered in the anterior chamber. What is this, and what else must be considered?
opts: Corneal blood staining
That is a late complication rather than this finding.
Hyphema, which can itself be a sign of open globe
Correct. It is not always an isolated injury.
Hyphema, which excludes an open globe
It does not exclude one.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage over the iris
That sits on the surface, not within the chamber.
Vitreous haemorrhage seen through the pupil
That lies behind the lens.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 27
set1.q: A partial-thickness lid laceration meets none of the referral criteria. How is it handled?
opts: Left open permanently to granulate
Not the described approach.
Closed with tissue adhesive and no follow-up
Follow-up is still arranged.
Referred to plastic surgery routinely
Ophthalmology follow-up is what is described.
Repair there, ophthalmology in 2 to 3 days
Correct. It does not need the specialist to close it.
Immediate transfer for operative repair
Not required for a partial-thickness cut.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 18
set1.q: Which examination shows the extent of a corneal abrasion?
opts: Slit lamp fluorescein
Correct. Fluorescein stains the exposed basement membrane.
Tonometry
Pressure does not map an epithelial defect.
Gonioscopy
That examines the drainage angle.
Dilated fundoscopy
The abrasion is on the surface.
Ocular ultrasound
It does not resolve an epithelial defect.

set1.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for common ophthalmological disorders by age
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 5
set1.q: In which population is ocular trauma the leading cause of monocular blindness, and why does that shape counselling?
opts: Adolescent girls, so sports goggles are the message
Not the group in which trauma leads.
Men over seventy, so driving assessment is the message
Not the group in which trauma leads.
Young adult men, so eye protection matters most
Correct. That is the group in which it leads.
Elderly women, so fall prevention is the message
Not the group in which trauma leads.
Infants, so childproofing is the message
Not the group in which trauma leads.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 39
set1.q: A traction retinal detachment is most commonly caused by what?
opts: Age-related macular degeneration
That damages the macula without traction detachment.
Retinitis pigmentosa
Not the described cause.
Uveal melanoma
A tumour is associated with the exudative type.
Blunt ocular trauma alone
Trauma accelerates the rhegmatogenous type.
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Correct. Fibrovascular tissue pulls the retina off.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 41
set1.q: A patient has numbness of the cheek after an orbital fracture. Which nerve is injured?
opts: The trochlear nerve
That affects the superior oblique.
The infraorbital nerve
Correct. Infraorbital numbness is a recognised finding.
The optic nerve
That would affect vision, not sensation.
The oculomotor nerve
That affects eye movement and the pupil.
The facial nerve
That affects movement rather than cheek sensation here.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17
set1.q: Which set of measures accompanies the shield in a suspected open globe?
opts: Antiemetics, analgesia, tetanus and computed tomography
Correct. Keeping the patient from straining protects the eye.
A mydriatic, tonometry and dilated fundoscopy of the retina
None of those is safe in a possibly open globe.
Copious irrigation and a pressure patch
Pressure risks extruding contents.
Topical anaesthetic drops to take home
Never sent home, in any eye injury.
Oral corticosteroids and observation
Not the described management.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 35
set2.q: What position is the patient placed in while awaiting repair of a retinal detachment?
opts: Lying on the affected side
Not the described position.
Head of bed elevated 30 to 40 degrees
Correct, alongside pain control and antiemetics.
Flat, with the head lower than the body
That is not the described position.
Prone with the face down
Not described here.
Sitting fully upright
More than the described elevation.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17
set2.q: An open globe injury is suspected. What is placed over the eye?
opts: A pressure patch
Pressure can extrude intraocular contents.
A saline-soaked gauze dressing
It provides no protection against pressure.
Nothing, so the eye can be re-examined
The eye needs protecting between examinations.
An ice pack held against the lid
Direct pressure is exactly what to avoid.
A rigid protective shield
Correct. It keeps pressure off the globe until repair.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
set2.q: Which feature makes computed tomography without contrast automatic after trauma?
opts: Loss of consciousness
Correct. It sits alongside alcohol, confusion, tachypnoea, apnoeic breathing, anticoagulants and eye penetration.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage alone
That alone does not mandate imaging.
Photophobia
A symptom rather than an imaging trigger.
Excessive tearing
A symptom rather than an imaging trigger.
A foreign body sensation
That points to the surface, not to imaging.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 36
set2.q: Which set of symptoms fits a retinal detachment?
opts: A curtain, floaters, flashes and a field defect
Correct. Cloudy or smoky vision belongs there too.
A painful red eye with a hazy cornea and haloes
That is acute angle closure.
Gradual painless loss of the peripheral field over years
That is chronic open-angle glaucoma.
Pain on eye movement with loss of colour vision
That is optic neuritis.
Bilateral disc swelling with transient obscurations
That is papilledema.

set2.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for common ophthalmological disorders by age
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 41
set2.q: A child has severe pain, bradycardia and vomiting on attempting to look up, but the eye looks quiet. What is this?
opts: A white-eyed blowout
Correct. In children entrapment may come with no orbital soft tissue signs at all.
Simple periorbital contusion
That does not produce autonomic disturbance on gaze.
Traumatic iritis
That does not produce bradycardia on eye movement.
A retrobulbar haemorrhage
That produces proptosis and a tense orbit.
Concussion without orbital injury
The gaze-provoked symptoms point to entrapment.

set2.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for common ophthalmological disorders by age
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 41
set2.q: A child with a quiet-looking eye vomits and becomes bradycardic each time he looks up after facial trauma. What does that combination represent?
opts: Gastroenteritis coinciding with the injury
That does not track eye movement.
Concussion alone
Concussion does not produce gaze-provoked bradycardia.
Muscle entrapment
Correct. Severe pain, bradycardia and vomiting on eye movement point to entrapment.
Raised intracranial pressure
That does not fire specifically on attempted upgaze.
Vasovagal response to pain
The trigger is eye movement specifically.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 16
set2.q: A foreign body sits in the posterior segment at initial evaluation. What is done?
opts: Leave it alone for now
Correct. Retrieving it early risks more damage to ocular structures.
Remove it immediately with forceps
That risks additional injury.
Remove it under topical anaesthetic
Anaesthesia does not reduce the structural risk.
Irrigate it out with balanced salt solution
Irrigation will not reach it and risks harm.
Apply a magnet to draw it forward
That is not the initial approach.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 41
set2.q: A patient has diplopia looking UP after a blow to the orbit. Which muscle is entrapped?
opts: Superior oblique
Not the entrapped muscle in a floor fracture.
Lateral rectus
Not the entrapped muscle described.
Levator palpebrae
That elevates the lid, not the globe.
Inferior rectus
Correct. Upward gaze diplopia means the inferior rectus or its supporting structures.
Medial rectus
That gives diplopia on lateral gaze.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 5
set2.q: Ocular trauma is the leading cause of monocular blindness in which group?
opts: Adolescent girls
Not the group in which trauma leads.
Men over seventy
Not the group in which trauma leads.
Young adult men
Correct. That is the group in which it leads.
Elderly women
Not the group in which trauma leads.
Children under five
Not the group in which trauma leads.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 16
set2.q: A laceration has cut the lens capsule. What happens to the lens?
opts: It is unaffected if the cut is peripheral
A capsular breach affects the lens wherever it sits.
It dislocates posteriorly in every case
Dislocation is not the described consequence.
It calcifies over several days
Calcification is not what follows.
It becomes hydrated, oedematous and opaque
Correct. Aqueous entering the capsule clouds it.
It hardens and darkens
That describes an age-related nuclear change.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 26
set2.q: A laceration sits 5 millimetres from the medial canthus. Why does that location matter?
opts: It cannot be closed surgically
It can be repaired, by the right person.
It indicates a basilar skull fracture
Different injury entirely.
The canalicular system may be transected
Correct. If it is not repaired properly the tearing is permanent.
The optic nerve runs immediately beneath
The nerve is not at that site.
It always indicates a globe rupture
It raises concern but does not establish rupture.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 21
set2.q: A patient who was grinding metal has vertical linear scratches across the cornea. What does that indicate?
opts: Evert the upper lid to find the object
Correct. Vertical linear defects mean it is in the tarsal conjunctiva of the upper lid.
Examine the lower fornix first
The vertical pattern points to the upper lid.
Order an orbital radiograph
The object is on the surface, not in the orbit.
Refer immediately for surgical exploration
It can be removed at the slit lamp.
Patch the eye and review in a week
The object needs removing now.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 33
set2.q: How is a periorbital haematoma decompressed?
opts: Intravenous mannitol alone
It does not drain orbital blood.
Observation until it resorbs
Not the management for a tense orbit.
Canthotomy with cantholysis
Correct. Release the lateral canthal tendon and cut its inferior branch so blood can drain.
Needle aspiration through the lid
Not the described procedure.
Pressure patching for 24 hours
Pressure is the wrong direction entirely.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 31
set2.q: What distinguishes an orbital contusion from a periorbital haematoma?
opts: Contusion involves the globe; the haematoma does not
Neither is defined by globe involvement.
Contusion is bilateral; the haematoma is unilateral
Laterality does not separate them.
Contusion follows sharp trauma; the haematoma follows blunt
Mechanism does not separate them.
Contusion needs surgery; the haematoma does not
That reverses the usual urgency.
Contusion has no haemorrhage; the haematoma bleeds in the orbit
Correct. The septum is what keeps the contusion in front of the eye.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17
set2.q: Why are antiemetics given alongside analgesia in a suspected open globe?
opts: They shorten the time to surgical repair
They do not affect operative scheduling.
Vomiting raises intraocular pressure
Correct. Keeping the patient from straining protects the eye.
They reduce the risk of endophthalmitis
They have no antimicrobial effect.
They lower the intraocular pressure directly
They act on nausea, not on pressure directly.
They allow the eye to be dilated safely
The eye is not dilated in trauma.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 35
set2.q: Which three factors bring a rhegmatogenous detachment forward?
opts: Sickle cell disease, burns and transfusion
Those relate to haemoglobinuria, not detachment.
Myopia, cataract surgery and ocular trauma
Correct. It is usually age-related, but these accelerate it.
Hyperopia, glaucoma and dry eye
Not the described risks.
Diabetes, hypertension and smoking
Those drive retinopathy rather than a retinal break.
Contact lens wear, allergy and blepharitis
Surface conditions, unrelated.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set2.q: What is the aim of hyphema management?
opts: Reducing photophobia
Comfort matters but is not the aim.
Preventing a rebleed
Correct. Every element of the regimen serves that.
Clearing the blood as fast as possible
Speed of clearance is not the goal.
Restoring accommodation
Not what management targets.
Preventing infection
Infection is not the primary concern here.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 44
set2.q: Clear fluid drips from a patient's nose after head trauma and leaves a ring within a ring on the bedsheet. What is this?
opts: A cerebrospinal fluid leak
Correct. Inner ring of blood, outer ring of cerebrospinal fluid.
Simple epistaxis
Blood alone does not form the double ring.
Lacrimal duct injury
Tears do not produce this pattern.
Purulent sinus drainage
Infection does not produce a double ring.
Cerebral oedema
Not a bedside finding of this kind.

set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
set2.q: Which action must be avoided whenever ocular trauma is suspected?
opts: Asking about tetanus status
That is required after penetration with metal or organic material.
Inspecting the periorbital tissues
Inspection is the first part of the examination.
Testing confrontation fields
That is appropriate in a cooperative patient.
Dilating the eye
Correct. It removes the pupil examination, one of the few windows onto the inside of the eye.
Checking visual acuity
Acuity is part of the assessment when the patient can cooperate.

set2.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for common ophthalmological disorders by age
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 41
set2.q: Which feature of orbital floor fracture is specific to children?
opts: Entrapment never occurs before adolescence
It does occur, and can be occult.
Children always have marked periorbital swelling
They may have none.
Children do not develop infraorbital numbness
Not the described distinction.
Children need no imaging
Imaging is still computed tomography.
Entrapment with no soft tissue signs
Correct — the white-eyed blowout.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set2.q: Which drugs should be avoided in a patient with hyphema?
opts: Cycloplegic drops
Cycloplegics are part of the regimen.
Topical corticosteroids
Corticosteroids are used.
Acetazolamide
It is used if the pressure is high.
Aspirin and antiplatelets
Correct. They raise the risk of a secondary haemorrhage.
Antiemetics
Antiemetics are given, so the patient does not strain.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43
set2.q: Why is surgery for an orbital fracture often delayed one to two weeks?
opts: To arrange outpatient anaesthetic review
Not the stated reason.
To let orbital swelling settle first
Correct. Operating into a swollen orbit raises the pressure further.
To allow the fracture to begin healing
Not the stated reason.
To complete a course of antibiotics
Antibiotics are for blood in the maxillary sinus.
To wait for the diplopia to resolve spontaneously
Not the stated reason.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 39
set2.q: Which type of retinal detachment is NOT treated primarily with surgery?
opts: All three are surgical
One of them is not.
None of the three is surgical
Two of the three are.
Exudative
Correct. With no break and no traction, treatment is directed at the underlying condition.
Rhegmatogenous
That is surgical.
Traction
That is surgical.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 44
set2.q: Which bedside test may be positive when cerebrospinal fluid is present?
opts: A pregnancy test
Unrelated to this fluid.
A dextrose stick
Correct. Cerebrospinal fluid contains glucose.
A urine dipstick for protein
Not the described test.
Fluorescein staining
That examines the cornea.
A rapid streptococcal antigen test
Unrelated to this fluid.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17
set2.q: At which sites does a globe most often rupture under blunt force?
opts: The macula and optic disc
Those are retinal structures, not the eye wall.
The lacrimal sac
It is not part of the globe.
Posterior to the muscle insertions, old incisions, the lamina cribrosa
Correct. Those are the weak points.
The central cornea and the visual axis, where the wall is thinnest
The central cornea is not the weak point.
The limbus alone
Rupture is not confined there.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
set2.q: A metal fragment may be lodged in the eye after grinding. Which study is ordered?
opts: Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit
A magnetic field can drag a metallic fragment through the eye.
Ocular ultrasound with pressure on the globe
Pressure risks extruding contents if the globe is open.
Plain orbital radiograph alone
It cannot localise the fragment adequately.
No imaging unless vision is reduced
Vision can be preserved with a retained fragment.
Computed tomography of the orbit
Correct. It answers the question without moving the fragment.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set2.q: Which condition raises the risk of complications from hyphema?
opts: Seasonal allergic rhinitis
It does not affect the risk.
Hypothyroidism
It does not affect the risk.
Migraine with aura
It does not affect the risk.
Iron deficiency anaemia
It is not the condition that raises the risk.
Sickle cell disease
Correct. It is specifically flagged as raising the risk.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 47
set2.q: Why are antibiotics for a cerebrospinal fluid leak controversial?
opts: They worsen the leak itself
They do not affect the leak.
They interfere with computed tomography
They do not.
They are contraindicated with a skull fracture
They are not contraindicated, merely debated.
They mask the halo sign
They do not affect the halo sign.
They risk selecting resistant organisms
Correct. That is the stated concern.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
set2.q: A nail is protruding from a patient's eye. What is done with it?
opts: Remove it only if the patient is stable
Stability does not change the risk.
Cut it flush with the cornea
Manipulating it at all risks the same extrusion.
Remove it under topical anaesthetic
Anaesthesia does not make removal safe here.
Leave it in place
Correct. It may be tamponading the wound, and removal can extrude intraocular contents.
Remove it and irrigate the tract
Removing it in the emergency department risks extrusion.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43
set2.q: Muscle entrapment is confirmed on computed tomography. Who is called, and why?
opts: Neurosurgery for admission
That is the basilar skull fracture pathway.
No consult; ice and analgesia suffice
That is the pathway for a fracture without entrapment.
Plastic surgery at the next elective list
Entrapment does not wait for an elective list.
A facial trauma surgeon urgently
Correct. A compromised blood supply is the reason for the urgency.
Ophthalmology within 2 to 3 days
Too slow for an entrapped muscle.
